newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Western Australia minister optimistic on gas.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Western Australia minister optimistic on gas.

text.p: Western Australia Energy Minister Colin Barnett on Thursday spoke optimistically about further expansion of the state's LNG export market, less than two months after expressing frustration over contradictory statements from the major players regarding the direction of the industry.

At a major energy conference in Perth, Barnett said "things have somewhat come together since then" and the government could see the potential for a 20 million tonne per year industry "for perhaps the next 20 to 100 years".

"A couple of months ago I had some sense of frustration which I expressed about what seemed to me to be a fairly untidy set of relations by various partners in both the North West Shelf and Gorgon joint ventures," Barnett said.

"It seems that things have somewhat come together since then," he said. "The North West Shelf has effectively gone down the path of expanding its project by two LNG trains and it is my understanding that right now relations between Gorgon and the North West Shelf are fitting into place," he said.
"There is no doubt, given our gas reserves and markets, that we can see the LNG export industry becoming Australia's major export industry," Barnett said.

Barnett also outlined his vision for the energy industry in Western Australia. He said he favoured greater public sector involvement in future power station development and operation but ruled out any move to privatise the new Collie power station for at least the next five years.

Barnett said he did not foresee any further re-structuring of Western Power - the state-owned electricity utility - but believed its future market area would be limited to the South West and possibly the Kalgoorlie mining district.

In the rest of the state he foresaw a trend towards increased tendering for reticulation of gas as a means of limiting the "ballooning" public sector losses in relation to supplying power to regional Western Australia.
He also signalled the best outcome for future ownership of the Dampier to Perth gas pipeline would be a 50-50 joint venture between stated owned Alinta Gas and the private sector.
"There is no doubt that pipeline is probably the single most important strategic asset in Western Australia," he said.
"While no option is closed off, my view is that the best outcome is some form of joint venture between private interests and Alinta Gas on some sort of 50-50 basis.
"That would be a good compromise. It would relieve Alinta Gas of substantial debt and bring private skills into the operation of the pipeline," Barnett said.

The partners in the North West Shelf project announced last month they would spend A$6 billion to expand to project to add about seven million tonnes per annum to the existing gas sales capacity of about 7.5 million tonnes a year.

Equal 16.66 percent shareholders in the project are Woodside Petroleum Ltd, BHP Petroleum (North West Shelf) Pty Ltd, BP Developments Australia Ltd, Chevron Asiatic Ltd, Shell Development (Australia) Pty Ltd and Japan Australia LNG (MIMI) Pty Ltd.

The partners in the nearby Gorgon field are negotiating with the North West Shelf partners to include Gorgon in the expansion. Chevron Corp, Texaco Inc and Royal Dutch/Shell Group each hold two-seventh stakes in Gorgon with Mobil Corp owning one-seventh.
